title: SAFE-DRIFT: Data Selection for Supervised Fine-tuning with Controllable Off-Target Drifts
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: Pure gradient alignment drifts along off-target directions and diversity alone doesn't prevent it; constraining updates balances both.
layout: 3 spectrum panels left-to-right after input stages; gradient arrow shows alignment-diversity tradeoff
description: The figure reads left to right. At far left, 'Initial Input' shows database icons for a large training dataset and a small target dataset, which yields a target gradient g_T. These feed an 'Enriched Dataset' 2-D scatter. Blue circles are training points and purple crosses are target points. A red vertical axis marks the reference 'forbidden' direction, and a dotted purple line marks the direction spanned by g_T. At right, under 'Data Selection', three rounded panels reuse the scatter: gradient-alignment methods, gradient alignment under constraints (labelled SAFE-DRIFT in orange-red), and diversity-targeting methods. Each panel has a black selected-gradient arrow, an orange angle θ, a dashed blue budget line, and a pink band showing the gradient's projection along the forbidden direction. The band is moderate in the first panel, narrow in the second and wide in the third. A red-to-blue gradient arrow below runs from importance of gradient alignment to importance of diversity. A legend box at the bottom explains the symbols.
caption: Trade-offs in data selection: gradient alignment selects candidate gradients aligned with the task but can cause substantial off-target drift (e.g., movement along a "forbidden dimension", in red). Diversity-based selection can mitigate this but does not reliably prevent off-target drift. \safe combines both approaches by constraining updates along the forbidden dimension.
abstract: We propose SAFE-DRIFT, a data-selection framework for supervised fine-tuning that improves a target capability while controlling unwanted drift in the model's other behaviors. We formalize this as a constrained optimization problem that maximizes alignment with the target gradient, subject to a budget on off-target drift which we quantify using the Fisher information of a reference distribution. Under this objective, the optimal, closed-form update is a damped natural-gradient step that downweights reference-sensitive directions. To estimate these high-dimensional gradients and work within the right geometry, we further derive a scalable algorithm that approximates the Fisher information and the target gradient in a shared low-dimensional subspace and analyze how entanglement of the target and reference task can affect the update. We evaluate SAFE-DRIFT against state-of-the-art data selection methods across diverse domains including coding and medical question answering, yielding competitive target performance while reducing degradation on specified off-target behaviors.
